Pilot report: network metrics from LIONESS personal networks

A review document: the pilot, its results, the spec, and the decisions log

Published

November 16, 2026

Summary

Scope. This document reports the pilot1 of proposal revision 1 (proposal.md, section 12): network metrics built from LIONESS personal networks (connectivity, strength, betweenness, eigenvector centrality, clustering, path length, efficiency, density, hub overlap), their stability over repeated visits, and whether the correction separates real structure from expression. It was built from project-spec.md, decisions.md, the saved results in pilot-e/results/, and, read-only, the GSE65391 description in pilot-d/results/; every number is computed from those files when the document renders.

Status. In STATUS.md the pilot is marked piloted-fail2. The closed form and the equivalence of edges and their formula held for every metric, and a module’s connectivity was its squared expression score; but the correction, which conditions on a five-gene interferon score, left the interferon set’s connectivity more stable than the cross connectivity, a deciding clause.

Pilot question Answer Key evidence
1. Do the closed forms hold? pass and pass Correlation of IFN connectivity with the squared IFN score 0.965 to 0.966 across cells; raw against first-order stability differed by at most 0.00039 over 76 metric-cell pairs.
2. More stable than edges, and the score’s stability? pass and pass IFN connectivity over IFN edges 0.104 (MCSE 0.0040); over the squared IFN score -0.0097 (MCSE 0.0012).
3. Does the correction separate real structure? fail and close call Corrected IFN connectivity over cross 0.094 to 0.151 (target within 0.05 of 0); corrected module connectivity over cross 0.056 (MCSE 0.0042).

What needs your decision (details in Action items and limitations): the status; whether to re-pilot with a correction that uses each module’s own score; and how the paper uses the finding that module connectivity is its squared expression score.

The idea

In plain language

A single LIONESS3 edge between two genes is noisy from one blood sample to the next, so the supervisor suggested looking at summaries of each person’s network instead: how strongly a group of genes is connected, how central a gene is, how far apart genes are. Summaries average many edges and should be steadier. But each edge is almost exactly the product of the person’s two gene levels, so the average edge inside a group of genes is almost exactly the square of the group’s average level. If the interferon4 genes sit 1 unit above average in a child, their connectivity is about 1; at 2 units it is about 4. This pilot simulates 131 children with six visits each and asks how stable each summary is, whether that stability is just the stability of the gene group’s squared level, and whether a corrected network removes the interferon part and keeps a real personal network.

Potential impact

LIONESS is used to build a network for each person (M. L. Kuijjer et al. 2019; Marieke L. Kuijjer et al. 2019); per-person network summaries such as weighted degree have been used as biomarkers, and the test-retest reliability of graph metrics is well studied for brain networks (Finn et al. 2015). Blood expression is partly person-specific (Whitney et al. 2003; Mishra et al. 2026), the lupus interferon signature is stable within patients (Petri et al. 2019), and cell composition drives much bulk co-expression (Farahbod and Pavlidis 2020).

The pilot shows that a module’s connectivity is, in practice, its squared expression score: the correlation was 0.965 to 0.966 in every cell, and the connectivity’s stability (0.247) matched that of the squared score (0.257) at the measured interferon stability (Table 3). Summaries were steadier than single edges, but because they track expression. Averaging did make a real personal module visible (0.095 against 0.027), which single edges hardly showed. A five-gene interferon score was not enough to correct connectivity (Figure 4). For users, the message is that a network summary should first be compared with the gene set’s own expression score.

Application: the study behind the data

The study

The data proposed for the application come from a longitudinal study of children with systemic lupus erythematosus5 (Banchereau et al. 2016), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2016.03.008, GEO series GSE653916, with repeated blood samples and disease activity at every visit. Table 1 gives the sizes and stabilities measured in this project, which set the simulation’s levels.

Why the stability of network metrics

The quantity is each metric’s intraclass correlation over a person’s visits. A metric is a candidate personal biomarker only if it is stable and carries more than the gene set’s own expression score.

Did the original study compute it?

No. The original study analysed expression modules; it built no single-sample networks and computed no network metrics.

In symbols

The mean standardized expression of a gene set \(S\) of size \(m\) in sample \(q\) (\(\bar z_{qS}\)) and its edges (\(e_{qij}\)) give the set’s connectivity (\(C_{qS}\)):

\[ \begin{aligned} C_{qS} &= \binom{m}{2}^{-1} \sum_{i < j \in S} e_{qij}, \\ C_{qS} &\approx \bar r_S + \frac{m}{m - 1}\, \bar z_{qS}^{\,2} - \frac{1}{m (m - 1)} \sum_{i \in S} z_{qi}^2 - \frac{\bar r_S}{m} \sum_{i \in S} z_{qi}^2 . \end{aligned} \]

Symbol Meaning
\(S\), \(m\) a gene set and its size
\(\bar z_{qS}\) mean standardized expression of the set in sample \(q\)
\(C_{qS}\) mean LIONESS edge within the set (connectivity)
\(\bar r_S\) mean reference correlation within the set

Line 2 averages the first-order edge over the pairs and uses \(\sum_{i<j} z_i z_j = \tfrac{1}{2}[(\sum z_i)^2 - \sum z_i^2]\). The leading varying term is the squared set score; the other terms are small for a set of 15 genes.

Critiquing the model

Any model is a simplification, and the useful question is not whether it is true but where it bends and whether the bend matters for the question being asked. The model above was chosen so that the problem could be written as a formula and checked by simulation, and each simplification that made that possible is a place where real data may behave differently. The table lists the main ones. Work through it one row at a time. The first column names the feature and the symbols in the equations that carry it, so find them there first. Then decide in your own words how the feature could fail for real data before reading the second column, and finally read the third column for what should be done to check it. Several of these checks are natural first tasks for the project. Which of them the pilot examined, and which it left open, is for you to find when you read the Methods and Results that follow.

Feature of the model Why it may not be realistic What should be done to check it
The correction conditions on a five-gene score A short score measures the factor with error and carries person-specific levels Use each set’s own leave-one-gene-out score
One threshold (absolute edge above 1) for the unweighted graph Density and clustering depend on the threshold Vary it, or use proportional thresholds
Distance as the inverse absolute edge Path metrics depend on the transform Compare with \(1 - \lvert e\rvert\)
45 genes Real networks are larger; path metrics change with size Repeat with hundreds of genes
Person gene levels independent across genes Real person-level differences are correlated Estimate from GSE65391
Six equal visits Real visits are irregular Mirror each child’s visits

Methods

Design

The pilot simulates 131 people with six visits each in 4 cells, as in pilot-d: an IFN factor on genes 1 to 20 with stability 0, 0.55, or 0.9, an observed cell-mix factor on genes 31 to 50, person gene levels, and a module of genes 21 to 30 that is personal in one cell. For every sample and edge type (raw LIONESS, first-order, partial-correlation given the IFN score of genes 1 to 5 and the cell mix), the network metrics of section 3 of the pre-registration are computed over genes 6 to 50, and each metric’s intraclass correlation over visits is estimated.

Part Cells Main factors Replicates
A, B 1 to 4 IFN stability 0, 0.55, 0.9; personal module 0 or 0.25 120 per cell

Known-answer checks

Known-answer checks come before any result, because every later number is only as good as the simulation that produced it. Each check sets up a case where the correct answer is known from theory, runs the simulation code on it, and compares the two. Agreement says nothing about the scientific question or about real data. It says that the code does what the model says. Disagreement means stopping to look for a bug before reading anything else, and the same checks apply to any code you write for the project.

Read each row of the table in four steps: the setting that was simulated, the known answer for that setting, what the simulation gave, and whether the gap between the two is small compared with the Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE). The MCSE is how much a simulated result moves from run to run because only a finite number of replicates was used. A gap within about two MCSE is noise, and a gap of several MCSE is a problem.

0 of 1 rows with a standard error are more than 2 MCSE from the known value.

Results

How to read the outputs

Each output traces back to a row of the design diagram (the captions name the part where one applies). Read each in the same four steps. First, find its row in the diagram, which says what was simulated and what was varied. Second, work out what one point or one table entry is, usually one combination of the varied factors, averaged over replicates. Third, identify the reference value that would hold if nothing were wrong, shown as a dashed or grey line wherever possible. Fourth, look for where the results leave that reference, and for which settings they do. The outputs report three kinds of quantity.

  • Bias is the average of an estimate minus its true value. When the truth is no difference, any average difference from 0 is a spurious difference created by the problem under study.
  • Level is how often a test rejects when there is truly nothing to find. A correct test at 0.05 rejects 5% of the time, so a rate above 0.05 means too many false alarms.
  • Power is how often a test rejects when there is a real effect. More is better, but only when the level is not inflated, because a test that rejects too often also looks powerful.

All rates and averages come from simulation, so each carries Monte Carlo error. That is why the figures show bars or a grey band, and why small differences should not be over-read.

This pilot reports intraclass correlations (0 when a metric changes completely between visits, 1 when it never changes) and correlations over samples.

Stability by metric

Figure guide (part B). Two panels, the measured interferon stability (cell 2) and the real personal module (cell 4). Each row is a metric; red points raw edges, purple first-order edges, blue the correction; the dashed line is the stability of the squared IFN score. Look for: whether red and purple coincide; whether the IFN connectivity sits on the dashed line; how far blue points move left; whether module connectivity moves right in cell 4.

Numbered findings

Each finding is a claim followed by the output behind it. Read the claim, open the output, and check that you can see the claim there before accepting it.

  1. A module’s connectivity is its squared expression score. The correlation over samples was 0.965 to 0.966 in every cell (Table 4, clause 1(a)), and the connectivity’s stability matched the squared score’s within -0.0097 (MCSE 0.0012) (clause 2(b)).
  2. Edges and their formula give the same stability for every metric. The largest difference over 76 metric-cell pairs was 0.00039 (clause 1(b)).
  3. Summaries are steadier than single edges. IFN connectivity was more stable than IFN edges by 0.104 (MCSE 0.0040) (clause 2(a)).
  4. The five-gene correction does not correct connectivity. The corrected IFN connectivity stayed more stable than the corrected cross connectivity by 0.094 to 0.151 (clause 3(a) fail); without any stable interferon it was 0.068 against 0.010 raw (decisions log, D2).
  5. The correction does steady the summing metrics. Density went from 0.144 raw to 0.082 corrected, near the null cell’s 0.079; path length from 0.100 to 0.055 (Table 3).
  6. Averaging reveals a real personal module. Module connectivity’s stability was 0.094 with the personal module against 0.026 without (clause 3(b), a close call).
  7. Betweenness, clustering, and hubs are barely stable. Their intraclass correlations stayed under about 0.08, hub overlap under 0.03 (Table 3).
  8. The known-answer checks hold (Table 2).

Proposal proposal.md, final 2026-11-16 (re-scope)

Written 2026-11-16
Status draft; section 3 completed after the verdict. The pregnancy spec is the record in git (git show c677b11:project-spec.md)

1. Question and why it matters

Question (one sentence): Over repeated blood samples of the same patient, how stable are her LIONESS edges, can they identify her, and do they predict her next disease activity, beyond her interferon level, her measured blood-cell counts, her gene levels, and the edges’ own first-order formula?

Why it matters: A personal network is a biomarker only if it is reproducible and carries something the cheap measures do not. If its stability is the person’s stable interferon level and her own gene levels, a user would measure those directly; if a corrected network keeps a stable personal part, that part is the candidate biomarker.

2. Mechanism we suspect

A LIONESS edge equals, to first order, \(r + z_{qi} z_{qj} - \tfrac{r}{2}(z_{qi}^2 + z_{qj}^2)\), so it carries the square of any factor that moves both genes. For a factor with within-person intraclass correlation \(\kappa\), the intraclass correlation of \(F^2\) is \(\kappa^2\) (proposal section 4), so edges of genes sharing a stable factor look personal with no personal co-expression; a factor that changes between visits adds within-person noise. Each person’s own stable gene levels enter the product term too, so every edge is partly person-specific through levels alone. The gap is zero for a factor with \(\kappa = 0\) (the null cell) and grows with \(\kappa\). If the mechanism is wrong, partial-correlation edges would keep the factor-driven stability, or edges and their formula would differ.

3. Pilot

Code: pilot-d/pilot.R (Rscript pilot-d/pilot.R --reps <n>), then Rscript pilot-d/verdict.R; data description Rscript pilot-d/describe_data.R.

Pass rule: pilot-d/preregistration.md, section 2.

Verdict file: pilot-d/results/verdict.rds, after the run.

Plot: pilot-d/results/stability.png.

Status: piloted-close-call (2026-11-16), 200 replicates per cell, 6 cells, three cores, 2,714 seconds; verdict file pilot-d/results/verdict.rds. Numbers rounded from pilot-d/results/cell_summaries.rds.

  1. Does the effect exist? Edges equal their formula in stability (largest difference under 0.0001; 1(b) pass). Stable interferon raised the interferon pairs’ stability (from about 0.07 to 0.14 at the measured level, 0.22 when very stable), but cross pairs rose too, and the pre-registered excess was 0.064 at the stress level, below 0.15 (1(a) fail).
  2. Large enough at the measured level? No: excess 0.016 (2(a) fail); the fix changed identification on interferon pairs by 0.004 (2(b) fail).
  3. Is there a fix? Yes: the fixed excess was 0.002 to 0.007 (3(a) pass), and the fix kept a real personal module (3(b) pass). Edges did not predict the next visit’s activity (concordance near 0.48; 3(c) fail in cell 6). Single-sample edges were unreliable over visits (intraclass correlation 0.07 to 0.22).

Pilot-e (network metrics, proposal section 12): piloted-fail (2026-11-16), 120 replicates per cell, 4 cells, 3,442 seconds; verdict file pilot-e/results/verdict.rds; numbers rounded from pilot-e/results/cell_summaries.rds.

  1. Closed forms: a module’s connectivity correlated about 0.97 with its squared expression score in every cell; raw and first-order edges gave the same stability for all 19 metrics (largest difference under 0.0004).
  2. Stability: IFN connectivity was more stable than IFN edges by about 0.10, and as stable as the squared IFN score (difference about -0.01).
  3. Correction: with the five-gene score, the corrected IFN connectivity stayed more stable than the cross connectivity by about 0.09 and 0.15 (fail); the corrected module connectivity exceeded the cross by about 0.056 with a real personal module (close call).

4. ADEMP skeleton

Aims. (1) How much of the stability of LIONESS edges over repeated samples comes from a stable shared factor? (2) Does a person’s network identify her, and is that identification the factor? (3) Do partial-correlation edges remove the factor’s part and keep a real personal network? (4) Do edges predict the next visit’s activity beyond the genes, and do they equal their formula throughout?

Data-generating mechanisms.

  • Factors varied: the IFN factor’s within-person intraclass correlation \(\kappa_F\) (0, 0.55 as measured, 0.9); a real personal module (\(\tau\) 0 or 0.25); visits per person (6, the GSE65391 median, or 3); whether activity changes the module.
  • Factors fixed, and why: 131 people (the GSE65391 children with two or more visits); 50 genes and the loadings of the first project; the cell-mix factor’s intraclass correlation 0.45 (measured 0.41 and 0.48) and activity’s 0.39; person-specific gene levels of variance 0.5 (people differ in level); normal noise.
  • A cell where the answer is known: the null cell, with no stable factor and no personal module.

Estimands. The intraclass correlation of each edge over visits; the excess of the factor pairs’ intraclass correlation over that of cross pairs (one factor gene, one module gene), which share the person-level gene effects but not the squared factor; fingerprinting accuracy; the concordance of next-visit activity predictions.

Methods compared. Raw LIONESS edges, first-order edges, partial-correlation LIONESS edges given the IFN score and the observed cell-mix factor; for prediction, \(R_0\), \(R_1\), E1, F1, N1 as in the first project, Gaussian elastic net, folds by person.

Performance measures. Mean intraclass correlation by pair group; fingerprinting accuracy; concordance; each with its MCSE.

Replicates and Monte Carlo SE target. 200 per cell if the time box allows; the MCSE of a mean intraclass correlation over 105 pairs is then well under 0.01.

5. Application

Dataset: GSE65391 (Banchereau et al. (2016)), GEO; the series matrix and the GPL10558 table in data/raw/, fetched by analysis/00_download.R, not committed.

Comparison: within each of the 131 children with two or more visits; 897 visits; the authors’ training (91 children) and test (40) split as a second check.

What to show: how much of a child’s network stability and identifiability is her interferon level, her cell mix, and her gene levels, and whether corrected networks predict her next disease activity.

Decisions log

This is the agent’s decisions.md for pilot-e, read from the file when the document renders.

D0. The literature pass

Proposal section 12 and the two searches of 2026-11-16 on LIONESS network metrics and the test-retest reliability of graph metrics. Nothing read since.

D1. The status call: piloted-fail, and what failed

The rule (pilot-e/preregistration.md) gives a fail because clause 3(a) failed in both cells: with partial-correlation edges, the interferon set’s connectivity stayed more stable than the cross connectivity (pilot-e/results/verdict.rds). Every other deciding clause passed: the closed form held (module connectivity correlated about 0.97 with the squared IFN score in every cell), and raw and first-order edges gave the same stability for all 19 metrics in every cell (largest difference under 0.0004). Clause 2(a) and 2(b) passed: connectivity was more stable than single edges, and exactly as stable as the squared IFN score. Clause 3(b) was a close call: the real personal module was visible in connectivity, at about the threshold.

There is no reading under which the rule passes: 3(a) is a deciding clause and missed by far more than its MCSE. What the fail says is specific (D2): the correction, conditioning on a five-gene IFN score, does not remove the IFN set’s shared signal once the edges are averaged into a connectivity. What it does not say: the closed forms, the equivalence, and the finding that connectivity is the squared expression score all held.

D2. Why the correction failed for connectivity

Two mechanisms, both visible in cell_summaries.rds.

  • The score measures the factor with error. The score averages five genes (1 to 5) that carry their own noise and their own person-specific levels. Residuals of genes 6 to 20 on that score keep a shared part of the factor; one edge carries it weakly, but connectivity averages 105 edges and keeps its square. The partial IFN connectivity’s stability rose with the factor’s stability (about 0.07, 0.14, 0.20 in cells 1 to 3).
  • The score carries person-specific levels. Even with no stable factor (cell 1), the partial IFN connectivity was more stable than the raw one: regressing every IFN gene on a score that holds the person’s own levels of genes 1 to 5 puts a shared person-stable term into all their residuals.

The theory section of the proposal anticipated the first (“the score’s measurement error leaves a residual”); its size at the module level was not computed. A correction using the module’s own score (each gene adjusted for the mean of the other genes of its set) would address both, but is a post hoc idea and would need its own pre-registration.

D3. What the metrics showed (reported, not judged)

  • Metrics that sum or average edges (strength, eigenvector centrality, efficiency, density, path length) became more stable as the IFN factor became more stable, and the correction brought most of them back to the null cell’s level (density, path length, strength).
  • Betweenness, local clustering, and hub overlap were barely stable in any cell (intraclass correlations under about 0.08; hub overlap under 0.03).
  • The real personal module raised its connectivity’s stability from about 0.03 to 0.09, for raw and corrected edges alike: averaging made a personal network visible that single edges hardly showed (pilot-d).

D4. The run

120 replicates per cell (the largest multiple of 20 that fitted the hour; amendment before the run), 3,442 seconds on three workers, one pass.

D5. What was not done

  • No metric was computed on GSE65391.
  • One threshold for the unweighted graph (absolute edge above 1); one distance (inverse absolute edge).
  • No prediction of the next visit’s activity.

Action items and limitations

Action items

  1. Decide the status. The rule gives piloted-fail, from the correction of connectivity (decisions log, D1 and D2).
  2. Decide whether to re-pilot with a correction that uses each gene set’s own score (D2), pre-registered before the run.
  3. Decide how the paper uses the closed form that a module’s connectivity is its squared expression score, which held in every cell.

Limitations

  • Everything here is simulation; no metric was computed on GSE65391.
  • One threshold and one distance transform; 45 genes.
  • No prediction of the next visit’s activity.

Footnotes

  1. A pilot is a quick, small first run of the proposal’s simulation, done before the project goes further, to check that the idea is worth the time. It asks three questions: does the effect exist, is it large enough at realistic sample sizes, and is there an obvious fix or diagnostic? The proposal (proposal.md) holds the pilot plan and its pass criteria.↩︎

  2. piloted-pass means all three pilot questions got a clear yes. piloted-fail means at least one clearly did not, so the project should not go on as proposed. piloted-close-call means at least one answer could be read either way, so the call is stated both ways: the reading that passes and the reading that fails.↩︎

  3. LIONESS (Linear Interpolation to Obtain Network Estimates for Single Samples) builds a network from all samples and again without one sample, and scales the difference to give that sample’s network.↩︎

  4. Interferons are signalling proteins of the immune system; many genes respond to them together, and their summed expression, the interferon score, is high in many patients with lupus.↩︎

  5. Systemic lupus erythematosus is an autoimmune disease that can affect skin, joints, kidneys, and blood, and often flares in pregnancy.↩︎

  6. The Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) is the public archive of the US National Center for Biotechnology Information for gene expression data; a series (GSE) holds one study’s samples.↩︎

  7. The AI agent that ran the pilot, wrote the files this document is built from, and kept a log of its decisions.↩︎
